lines: This abstraction's own documentation gives a specific example: one wrapper first, then a cap on how many run at once, admits a lot more work at once than the reverse order.
Does real code actually behave that way, or is that just a simplification written into the documentation?
answer: The documentation's own numbers hold up when you actually run it.

lines: Run it for real: with the first wrapper in front, well over a hundred requests were accepted right away;
with the order reversed, only exactly ten were — matching the documentation's own claim closely.
Build a real pipeline with a deliberately slow authorization step, and a real deadline wrapped around the whole thing, authorization included.
Does a slow authorization step get caught by that deadline, the same way a slow piece of work would?
answer: The deadline bounds whatever sits inside it, authorization included.

lines: Run it for real: the real deadline fired well before the slow authorization step would have finished on its own,
because it wrapped that step too, not only the work behind it.
steps.takeaway: A deadline bounds whatever it actually wraps; placed around a slow step too, it genuinely catches that.

lines: Now put that same deadline only around the work behind authorization, with the slow authorization step run ahead of it, outside its reach.
Does the slow authorization step still get caught, since the deadline is still somewhere in the pipeline?
answer: The deadline never sees the authorization step at all; only what it actually wraps.

lines: Run it for real: with the deadline moved inside, the slow authorization step ran all the way to completion, entirely unbounded,
taking far longer than the deadline's own limit — because the deadline never saw it at all.
steps.takeaway: The same deadline bounds a different thing depending on where it sits; move it, and the protection moves with it.

lines: Wrap a piece of work that isn't safe to run twice in a real retry wrapper, with nothing guarding it.
It fails twice, then succeeds on the third attempt.
How many times does its own side effect actually run?
answer: Nothing stopped the side effect from running again, each time it was retried.

lines: Run it for real: the work's own side effect ran three separate times, once per attempt,
including the two attempts that failed, since nothing was guarding it from running again.
steps.takeaway: Retrying work that isn't safe to run twice means its side effect runs again, every time, unless something stops it.

lines: Add one real check to that same piece of work, one that remembers it already ran, with the same two failures and the same retries.
The side effect now runs exactly once. One check, and all those repeats stopped mattering.
So, pulling this topic together: a real wrapper placed first admits far more work at once than the reverse order, matching the documentation's own numbers.
A deadline bounds whatever it actually wraps, and moving it changes what it protects.
And a piece of work that isn't safe to run twice reruns its own side effect on every retry, unless a real check remembers it already ran.
